opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so thermal cameras were one of those things that looked simple on paper and turned out to be a constant source of pain. The big lesson for me was that in hardware, the failure is almost never where you first look.

You'd get a report that a robot's thermal feed was dropping out or producing garbage frames, and your instinct as a software person is to look at the driver, the firmware, the image pipeline. Sometimes it was that. But a lot of the time it turned out to be something physical and boring: a connector that wasn't fully seated and would lose contact when the robot vibrated over rough ground, a cable flexing at the same point a thousand times a day until it cracked internally, or the sensor itself drifting because the enclosure got hotter than anyone had planned for. With a thermal camera that's a nasty one, because heat in the housing literally corrupts the thing you're trying to measure.

So a few things stuck with me.

First, intermittent failures are the worst kind, and they're usually mechanical or environmental. If something fails consistently, you can find it on your bench in an afternoon. If it fails one time in five hundred, and only in the field, it's almost always vibration, temperature, moisture, or a marginal connection. You have to build the conditions that reproduce it: shake tables, thermal chambers, actually running the thing outdoors for days, not just testing it on a desk.

Second, logging is everything. Early on we'd get a robot back and have basically no idea what happened. Once we started logging much more aggressively, things like sensor temperatures, reset counts, frame drop rates, and voltage on the rails, patterns jumped out right away. You'd see that failures clustered on hot afternoons, or on one batch of units, and suddenly a mystery became an obvious root cause.

Third, design for graceful degradation. The camera is going to fail at some point, so the question is what the robot does when it does. Does the whole system hang because one USB device stopped responding? Or does it detect it, power-cycle that sensor, and keep going in a degraded mode? A lot of reliability isn't making components never fail. It's making the system resilient to the failures you know are coming.

And honestly, that mindset carries over to working with AI systems now. You assume the individual pieces will sometimes be flaky, you instrument everything so you can actually see what went wrong, and you design the overall loop so it can recover instead of falling over.

r001.rationale: The response discusses loose connectors and cable fatigue as possible causes, but does not state that USB cables with identical specifications can have different reliability.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that was at Cobalt Robotics, where we built security robots that patrolled office buildings overnight. The thermal camera was one of a dozen sensors on the robot, and the pattern we kept seeing was that it would work perfectly in the lab, work perfectly for the first few weeks in the field, and then fail in ways that were really hard to reproduce.

The first lesson was that the failure almost never came from the component you thought it would. We'd suspect the camera itself, swap it, and the problem would come back. It turned out to be things like a connector that would loosen slightly after a few thousand cycles of the robot hitting a bump in the carpet, or a USB hub that would brown out when the motors drew peak current at the same moment the camera was streaming. None of that shows up on a bench.

The second lesson was about visibility. Early on we didn't have good telemetry on the sensor layer. We'd get a report that the robot "wasn't seeing well" and have no way to tell if the camera dropped out, if the driver hung, or if the image was there but garbage. Once we started logging frame rates, temperatures, and reconnect events for every sensor, the whole category of mysterious failures got a lot less mysterious. You can't fix what you can't observe.

And the third thing, which I think generalizes way beyond robots, is that reliability is a property of the whole system over time, not of any individual part. Every component we used had a datasheet that said it was fine. The system still failed. You have to design for the parts failing, so the robot keeps doing something useful when the thermal camera drops, instead of the whole patrol falling over.

I actually think about that a lot now with agents. When Claude Code is running a long task, individual tool calls fail all the time. The question is whether the system notices, recovers, and keeps going, or whether one flaky step takes down the whole thing. That instinct came straight from watching robots fail at two in the morning.

r001.rationale: The response mentions a loosening connector and a USB hub brownout, but does not state that USB cables with identical specifications can differ in reliability.

astra-6.text:
It taught me that reliability is a system property. A camera can work perfectly on the bench, and then you put it on a robot with vibration, temperature changes, and imperfect power, and suddenly it’s unreliable. The symptom might look like a software bug, but the cause could be a connector or a power issue.

So you have to make failures observable. Can you tell whether the camera stopped sending frames, whether the connection dropped, or whether the process crashed? And then you need a way to recover. Getting the robot to work once is very different from getting it to work every day without someone standing next to it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions connectors and power as possible causes of camera failures, but does not state that USB cables with identical specifications can have different reliability.

sol-6.1.text:
It taught me to think about reliability as a property of the whole system. When a camera stops producing useful data, the sensor is only one possible cause. You have to work through power, connections, software, and the conditions the robot is operating in.

And an intermittent failure is especially hard, because getting it working again doesn’t mean you understand it. You need enough instrumentation to capture what happened, a way to reproduce it, and then a test that tells you whether the fix actually worked. That changes your definition of done: it has to keep working under the conditions it will encounter in the field.

r001.rationale: The response discusses system-level reliability and possible causes such as power and connections, but does not state that USB cables with identical specifications can differ in reliability.
